title: Writing a Letter
short: A letter has the date, a greeting ("Dear Ms. Grant,"), the body in short paragraphs, a closing ("Sincerely," or "Warmly,") and your signature.
trouble: Learners pick a closing that doesn't fit: "Love" for a business letter or "Yours truly" for a grandmother. Match the closing to how well you know the reader.

blocks.html: A thank-you note is a short letter. Longer letters, to a landlord, a school, a company or a grandparent, use the same frame with a body in the middle.
A letter has the date, a greeting ("Dear Ms. Grant,"), the body in short paragraphs, a closing ("Sincerely," or "Warmly,") and your signature. Match the closing to how well you know the reader.

The frame tells the reader at a glance when the letter was written, who it is for and who sent it, which matters when letters are filed or answered weeks later. Short paragraphs, one idea each, make the request easy to find. The closing sets the tone: "Sincerely" is respectful for anyone; "Love" belongs to family and close friends.

blocks.title: Choosing a closing
blocks.q: Mia writes to her landlord about a broken heater. Which closing fits: "Love," "Sincerely," or "See ya,"?
steps: A landlord is a business contact.
"Sincerely," is respectful and fits any formal letter.

blocks.title: One idea per paragraph
blocks.q: Sam's letter to a college office mixes a thank-you, a question about deadlines and his schedule into one long paragraph. How can he fix it?
steps: He gives each idea its own short paragraph.
First the thank-you, then the question, then his schedule.
The reader can now find the question at once.
blocks.a: Split it into short paragraphs, one idea each.

blocks.html: Picking a closing that doesn't fit: "Love" for a business letter or "Yours truly" for a grandmother. Match the closing to how well you know the reader; when unsure, "Sincerely" or "Best regards" is safe.
